segments.text: Jetlag doesn't just make you tired. It can affect your brain. Let me explain. Last time I traveled to Asia, we measured my biomarkers. Here's what came back. It took 9 days to re-stabilize my blood glucose, 9 days to retrain my circadian rhythm, and 18 days for full sleep architecture recovery. Here's why.

Your body runs on a clock. The big hand is sleep, and the little hand is sunlight. Cross enough time zones, and that clock is busted. Research shows repeated frequent flying and jetlag is linked to disruptions in brain regions involved in memory, higher rates of anxiety, depression, and alcohol use. On top of that, flying suppresses melatonin for hours after you land. Avoiding travel entirely is unrealistic, but here's what I recommend. Aim for no more than one international trip every 3 months. Plan for 1 day of recovery per time zone crossed. On long flights, try to align your sleep with your destination's time zone. Hydrate during

flights. Cabin humidity can drop as low as 5%, which is drier than the Sahara Desert. Friends, seeing the world is a wonderful thing. Also, know that your biomarkers will experience some heavy layovers.
